# Text

```{r}
#| include: false
source("../R/setup.R")
```

Which point is which? `text` draws a **string**, a piece of text such as a name
or a number, at each `(x, y)` position. It is `point`'s sibling: both place one
glyph per row. A point's glyph is a dot by default. A text mark's glyph is a
string, and that string comes from a column, through the `label` channel. This
chapter uses it four ways: to name the points of a scatter, to print a value on
a bar, to write a note on a plot, and to name the parts that a transform places,
such as the nodes of a network.

Every plot in this chapter is drawn on a white panel, with
`theme(background = "white")`, instead of gog's light gray. Dark letters and
gray dots are easier to read on white. [The panel's
background](../style.qmd#the-panels-background) shows the setting.

## The mark and its content {#the-mark-and-its-content}

A point tells you *where* a row is; it cannot tell you *which* row. The `medals`
table holds five countries, one row each, with the number of `gold`, `silver`
and `bronze` medals each country won. Drawn as dots, the five countries are five
points with nothing to say which country is which:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(medals)
```

```{r}
data(medals) + point + x(gold) + y(silver) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Five countries, and no names") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: points, x is gold, y is silver."*

Replace `point` with `text` and bind `label` to `country`, and each row's name
is drawn at its position:

```{r}
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same five, named") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country."*

That is the main difference between the two marks. `point` draws the same dot
at every row's position. `text` draws one of the row's own values there instead.

## Both at once: the labeled scatter {#both-at-once-the-labeled-scatter}

A dot marks one position on the panel. A word is much wider than a dot, so a
name on its own only shows roughly where its row is. The two marks can be
drawn together: layer a `point` mark and a `text` mark on the same `x` and `y`,
with the `+` [operator](../operators.qmd). The dot gives the exact position and
the string gives the name. That is a labeled scatter, built from two marks
rather than a third mark of its own.

Each `style()` applies to the mark written before it. So
`style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e")` sets the dots' size and colors them a
medium gray. The words keep their own size and color. Without a nudge, each label is drawn centered on its dot, and the word hides the
dot, as on the left. `style(nudge = "up")` moves every label above its dot, as
on the right:

```{r}
((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
    text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
    x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
    title("No nudge: each name sits on its dot") +
    theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "up") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
     title('nudge = "up": named just above') +
     theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 420)
```

*"Given the medals: points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by
country, beside points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country,
with nudge up."*

### Nudging the label off its point {#nudging-the-label-off-its-point}

Up is only one of four directions, and it is not always the side with room. A
dot with a neighbor just above it has no space for its name there. Those labels
need a different direction.
`style(nudge = )` shifts a text label off its `(x, y)`. It takes one direction:
`"up"`, `"down"`, `"left"`, or `"right"`:

```{r}
(((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
    text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "up") +
    x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "up"') +
    theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "down") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "down"') +
     theme(background = "white"))) /
  ((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "left") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "left"') +
     theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "right") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "right"') +
     theme(background = "white")))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 760)
```

*"Given the medals: points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by
country, with nudge up, beside points and also text, x is gold, y is silver,
label by country, with nudge down; above points and also text, x is gold, y is
silver, label by country, with nudge left, beside points and also text, x is
gold, y is silver, label by country, with nudge right."*

You do not give a distance. The engine sets it from each label's own font size,
far enough that the word does not touch a dot of the default size. That is why
`nudge` asks only for a direction, and every label moves in that one direction.
`jitter` and `dodge` work differently: they
compute each mark's offset from the data, so marks can move by different
amounts. Only `text`
accepts a nudge. A `point` or a `bar` has no label to move, so the engine
refuses the setting there and names the mark that does.

### `repel`: moving labels off each other {#repel-moving-labels-off-each-other}

A nudge shifts every label the same way, so it moves each label off its own dot
and does nothing else. When the labels collide with *each other*, they all
move together and still overlap. Thirty European
countries are enough to show it. The `gm_europe` table holds them, one row per
country in 2007, with each country's GDP per person (`gdp`), life expectancy
(`life`) and `population`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_europe)
```

```{r}
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Thirty countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder Europe: points and also text, x is gdp, y is life, label by
country."*

Every name is centered on its own dot, and where the countries crowd together the
words overlap. Germany, Belgium, Finland and the United Kingdom have almost the
same `gdp` and `life`, so their four names are drawn on top of one another.

`repel` solves that. It is one of the four collision modifiers, with `jitter`,
`dodge` and `stack`, so it is written after the mark with `*`, not inside
`style()`. It measures where the labels and the dots actually are, then moves
each label off the words around it:

```{r}
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same thirty, moved apart") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder Europe: points and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is
life, label by country."*

Notice three things in this plot. Every label is drawn just outside its dot, so
no word covers the dot it names. A label with other words near it moves to
whichever side has room. A label with space around it stays directly above its
dot. The first two follow from one rule: `repel` pulls each label toward its own
dot, and pushes it away from every other word and every dot, its own included.
The third follows from where `repel` starts. A plain label is centered on its
dot, but `repel` starts every label just above its dot, so a label with nothing
near it stays there.

In a more crowded plot, `repel` can move a label much further from its dot. Once
the gap is larger than the height of one line of text, gog draws a thin line
from the dot to the word, so you can still see which dot the name belongs to. No
label in this plot moved that far, so none has a line.

The placement is **deterministic**. It uses no random-number generator and does
not read the computer's clock, so the same sentence draws the same picture
every time. It does depend on the order of the rows, though. `repel` settles the
overlaps pair by pair, in the order of the rows, so the same rows in a different
order can end with some labels in different places.

Sometimes no placement keeps every label apart. `repel` then still draws every
label, and gog prints a message saying how many still overlap. Which names to
leave out is your decision, so `repel` never removes one. In this plot all
thirty fit, so gog prints no message.

`gapminder_2007` holds the same columns as `gm_europe` for all 142 countries in
2007:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

The same sentence with this table names all 142 countries, and they do not all
fit. In `theme()`, `grid = "none"` also leaves out the gridlines, so they do not
run through the crowded labels:

```{r}
#| message: true
data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("All 142 countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white", grid = "none")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is
life, label by country."*

Every country is named, but three labels still overlap another one, and the
message says so. Many labels moved far from their dots, so gog drew a thin line
from each of those dots to its name.

Three things give crowded labels more room, and the message names all three:
fewer rows, a smaller `style(size = )`, and a larger plot. `theme(width =, height =)` sets the plot's
size in pixels, and the
[Composition](../composition.qmd#how-thin-is-the-marginal-histogram-themewidth-height)
chapter explains it.

Fewer rows is often the right choice. On a large table you usually name only the
few rows that matter: give the `text` layer its own table that holds just those
rows, as [A note is a layer](#a-note-is-a-layer) does with one row. In the web
edition, clicking a dot on a plot with `brush()` shows its values beside it,
which [Selection](../selection.qmd#stamping-a-point) calls a stamp. Stamps help
you choose those rows. A stamp is gone when the page reloads, while a `text`
label is part of the sentence and is drawn every time.

In the next plot, the dots come from `gapminder_2007` again. The names come from
`gm_populous`, the ten countries with the most people in 2007. It has the same
columns, so the `text` layer reads `gdp` and `life` from it:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_populous)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The ten most populous of 142 countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, and also
text from the ten most populous countries, derived by repel, label by
country."*

The `gdp` axis uses a log scale ([Scales](../scales.qmd)), which gives the many
poorer countries more room. `repel` moves the names off the 132 unnamed dots
too, though the dots and the names come from different tables. It moves a name off those dots only a
little, never far enough for gog to draw a thin line. So a name can still cover
some of them: United States covers several at the top right, and Bangladesh
covers two. A [halo](#a-halo-around-each-label) keeps such a name readable.

A nudge and `repel` can be used together, and each does one job.
`style(nudge = )` chooses the side each label is pulled toward, and `repel` then
moves the labels that still overlap:

```{r}
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Nudged right first, then moved apart") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder Europe: points and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is
life, label by country, with nudge right."*

With every label pulled to the right of its dot, four labels run into their
neighbors there, and `repel` moves those four far enough to need a thin line.
Norway's dot is at the right edge of the panel. `repel` keeps every label inside
the panel, and unlike a plain label it does not widen the axis to make room. So
Norway's label is moved back over its own dot.

## Number labels: the value on each mark {#number-labels-the-value-on-each-mark}

A label does not have to be a name, and it does not have to be drawn on a scatter. A
bar shows which country won more gold medals. To read how many more, a reader has to measure
each bar against the axis, and that measurement is only an estimate. Sometimes
the number itself is the answer. Bind a column that holds numbers and each row's
value is drawn. By default, a whole number is printed without a decimal point,
and any other number is rounded to at most three decimal places. Layer `text`
over `bar` to print each bar's height. Without a nudge, each number is centered
on its bar's top edge, and the edge crosses the digits. `style(nudge = "up")`
moves each number just above its bar:

```{r}
data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") +
  text + x(country) + y(gold) + label(gold) + style(nudge = "up") +
  y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: bars and also text, x is country, y is gold, label by gold,
with nudge up."*

Each bar now carries its number, so the difference between the USA's 46 and
China's 38 can be read without the axis.

The medals table already holds the numbers. A bar chart that counts rows
computes its numbers itself. In `bar * count`, the
[`count`](../transforms.qmd#count-frequency-aggregation) transform writes the
number of rows in each bar into a column called `count`. `text * count` uses the
same transform, so `label(count)` can print that column on each bar. The
`count` column is not in `gapminder_2007`. The transform writes it, so only a
layer that runs the transform can name it. [The column each transform
writes](../transforms.qmd#the-column-each-transform-writes) lists the column
each transform writes. As in the medals plot, the numbers are nudged up:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  text * count + label(count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its count") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, and also text
derived by count, label by count, with nudge up."*

Africa's bar is labeled 52, and Oceania's bar is labeled 2.

To draw the bars horizontally, put the category on `y` instead of `x`. Each bar
is then drawn from left to right, and the counts are on the `x` axis. The text
layer reads the same positions, so each number is centered on the right end of
its bar. The nudge points in the direction the bars grow, so it is now
`style(nudge = "right")`, which moves each number just past that end:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + y(continent) +
  text * count + label(count) + style(nudge = "right") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, y is continent, and also text
derived by count, label by count, with nudge right."*

Africa's 52 is past the end of the longest bar, and Oceania's 2 is past the
shortest. The axis already reaches a little past the longest bar, and Africa's
52 fits in that room. A label that would not fit inside the panel widens its
axis instead
([Scales](../scales.qmd#the-axis-fits-your-data)).

A histogram is labeled the same way. The
[`bin`](../transforms.qmd#bin-histogram) transform also writes a column called
`count`, the number of rows in each bin. So `text * bin` with `label(count)`
prints how many countries fall in each bin of life expectancy:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) +
  text * bin + label(count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life, and also text derived by
bin, label by count, with nudge up."*

The last bin, from about 78 to 83 years, holds the most countries: 32.

Add `proportion` to both layers, and each bar is a share of all the countries
instead of a count. `bin` writes a `count` column, and `proportion` then turns
each count into a share, so the rows hold a column called `proportion` and no
`count`. The text layer therefore names `label(proportion)`:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(proportion, decimals = 2) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and proportion, x is life, and also
text derived by bin and proportion, label by proportion with 2 decimal places,
with nudge up."*

The last bin is now labeled 0.23. Its 32 countries make a share of 0.2254 of the
142, and `decimals = 2` rounds the share to two decimal places. `decimals` is
explained a few plots below, where each continent's mean life expectancy is
printed. These rows hold
no `count`, so `label(count)` is refused, and the message names the transform
that replaced it:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(count)
```

After `count`, `bin` or `proportion` there is one row for each bar. A label can
print only a column those rows hold. In `bar * count + x(continent)`, those rows
hold two columns, `count` and `continent`. Each row is a whole continent, so it
holds no `country` to print:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  text * count + label(country)
```

After a summary such as `mean`, there is also one row for each bar. In
`bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life)`, each of those rows holds its continent's
mean, written into `life` itself. A summary is given a column to reduce, here
the `life` named on `y`, so its answer replaces that column. `count`, `bin` and
`proportion` are given no column, so they write a new column with a name of
their own. So `text * mean` with `label(life)` prints each continent's mean life
expectancy:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  text * mean + label(life) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, and also
text derived by mean, label by life, with nudge up."*

Asia's mean, 70.72848, is printed as 70.728. For `sum`, `median`, `max`, `min`
and `quantile`, write `label()` with the column the summary reads.

Asia's label, 70.728, has more decimal places than this plot needs. You cannot
round a mean before gog computes it, so `label()` takes the number of decimal
places to print. `label(life, decimals = 1)` prints Asia's mean as 70.7:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  text * mean + label(life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, and also
text derived by mean, label by life with 1 decimal place, with nudge up."*

Each label now has one decimal place, from Africa's 54.8 to Oceania's 80.7. Every
label gets exactly one decimal place, so a mean of exactly 77 would print as
77.0, and all five labels show the same precision. `decimals = 0` rounds each
mean to a whole number, so Asia's prints as 71. gog reads a categorical column
as names, not numbers, so there is no number to round, and
`label(country, decimals = 1)` is refused:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country, decimals = 1)
```

A sum can be a very large number. `bar * sum` with `y(population)` adds up the
people of each continent, and `label(population)` prints Asia's sum in full, as
3811953827. A number that long is hard to read. `label(population, short = TRUE)`
prints it short, with K for thousands, M for millions, B for billions (a thousand
millions) and T for trillions (a million millions):

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +
  text * sum + label(population, short = TRUE) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum, x is continent, y is population, and
also text derived by sum, label by population written short, with nudge up."*

Asia's label is now 3.81B, and Oceania's is 24.5M. A short number keeps three
significant digits. `decimals` sets the number of decimal places instead, so
`label(population, short = TRUE, decimals = 1)` prints 3.8B for Asia. An axis
takes `short` too: `y(population, short = TRUE)` takes each tick's letter from
the tick's own size, as
[Scales](../scales.qmd#percent-short-and-decimals-writing-the-numbers) shows.
Without `short`, an axis chooses one letter for all its ticks from the distance
between them. Here the ticks are a billion apart, so the axis already writes 1B,
2B, 3B and 4B, and `short` would change nothing.

A share can be printed as a percent. `label(proportion, percent = TRUE)` prints
the last bin's share, 0.2254, as 22.5%:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(life) +
  y(proportion, percent = TRUE) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(proportion, percent = TRUE) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and proportion, x is life, y is
proportion written as a percent, and also text derived by bin and proportion,
label by proportion written as a percent, with nudge up."*

The axis takes the same argument on `y(proportion)`, so the axis and the labels
are written the same way. Without `decimals`, a percent keeps one decimal place
and leaves it off when it is 0, so a share of 0.190 prints as 19%, not 19.0%.
`percent` and `short` cannot be used together, because they are two ways to
write one number. The message asks you to keep one of them:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(proportion, percent = TRUE, short = TRUE)
```

`label()` prints a column of dates as dates, such as 2024-03-01, and a column
of date-times with the hour and minute, such as 2024-03-01 14:05. A date is not
written as a number, so gog refuses `decimals`, `short` and `percent` on it.

After `bin * cumulative`, each bin holds two numbers: its own count, and the
total so far. [`cumulative`](../transforms.qmd#cumulative-the-running-total)
writes the total to a column named `cumulative`, and the `count` column that
`bin` wrote stays beside it. So `label(cumulative)` prints the height of each
bar, and `label(count)` prints each bin's own count on the same bar:

```{r}
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(life) +
    text * bin * cumulative + label(cumulative) + style(nudge = "up") +
    title("label(cumulative): the running total") +
    theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(life) +
      text * bin * cumulative + label(count) + style(nudge = "up") +
      title("label(count): each bin on its own") +
      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 420)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and cumulative, x is life, and also
text derived by bin and cumulative, label by cumulative, with nudge up, beside
bars derived by bin and cumulative, x is life, and also text derived by bin and
cumulative, label by count, with nudge up."*

The bars, and the places of the labels, are the same in both plots, because `x`
and `y` place a label and `label` chooses only the number it shows. On the left,
each number is the bar's height, so it matches the `y` axis: the last bar
reaches 142. On the right, the numbers do not match the `y` axis, and that is
not a mistake. Each is the count of one bin: 32, the last, is 142 minus the 110
before it.

### Labels on dodged bars {#labels-on-dodged-bars}

With [`dodge`](../transforms.qmd#dodge-side-by-side-instead-of-on-top), grouped
bars set one bar per group side by side in each **slot**, the stretch of the
axis that belongs to one category. A label layer
without `dodge` prints all of a slot's numbers in its middle, between the bars.
With the same `dodge` and a split of its own, each label is printed on its own
bar. The `gm_eras` table holds two years, 1957 and 2007, with one row per country
in each:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gm_eras)
```

`color(era)` is written after `bar`, so it colors the bars alone
([Encoding scope](../encoding-scope.qmd)). [`group(era)`](../channels.qmd#group)
splits the labels by era without coloring them:

```{r}
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  text * mean * dodge + group(era) + label(life, decimals = 1) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is
life, colored by era, and also text derived by mean and dodge, grouped by era,
label by life with 1 decimal place, with nudge up."*

Each continent has two labels, one on each era's bar. Africa's 41.3 is on its
1957 bar, and its 54.8 is on its 2007 bar. A `text` layer with `dodge` is
refused when nothing splits it, because it then has no groups to set side by
side. `color(era)` belongs to the bars alone, so without `group(era)` the text
layer has no split. The message names `color` and `group` as the two ways to add
one:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  text * mean * dodge + label(life, decimals = 1)
```

## Color {#color}

You see a hue faster than you can read a word, so a color split shows you the
groups before you read a single name. Every label so far has been printed in one
color, which is the default. Map a categorical column to `color` and the labels
split by that column. A continuous column on `color` is refused on a text mark,
and the message suggests `size` or `opacity` instead, as [What it
refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows. The mapping
gets a legend to name the groups, and the colors come from the same palette
that points and bars use. In the plot below each country is its own group, so the hue
repeats the name:

```{r}
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + color(country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("One hue per country") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, color by
country."*

The legend names the five hues. A column whose value several rows share, such
as `continent`, is more useful: one hue marks every name in a group before you read
any of them. The `gm_populous` table, shown in [`repel`: moving labels off each
other](#repel-moving-labels-off-each-other), has such a column. Its ten
countries come from three continents:

```{r}
data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  label(country) + color(continent) +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the ten most populous countries: text derived by repel, x is gdp on a
log scale, y is life, label by country, color by continent."*

The six Asian names share one hue, the three from the Americas share another,
and Nigeria is the only name in a third hue.

## Styling: one color, one size {#styling-one-color-one-size}

The `color` channel takes its hues from a column. When the words are the whole
plot, with no dots or bars beside them, you may want one color of your own and a
larger font. The default size, 13 pixels, is often too small to read
comfortably.
Neither comes from a column, so both are settings rather than mappings.
`style(color = )` sets the color of the words, and `style(size = )` sets the
font size in pixels. Each applies to every label in the layer:

```{r}
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Bigger, greener labels") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, colored
seagreen, with size 17."*

A setting gives every label in the layer the same font size. To size each label
by a value of its own, map a column instead, as the next section shows.

## Sizing and fading labels by a column {#sizing-and-fading-labels-by-a-column}

`size` and `opacity` are channels on `text`, as they are on `point`. A mapped
`size` draws each label at a font size from 8 to 24 pixels. The smallest value
gets 8, the largest gets 24, and the others fall in proportion between them.
Here, the more bronze medals a country won, the larger its name:

```{r}
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + size(bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Each name sized by its bronze medals") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, size by
bronze."*

The legend shows the letter *a* at three sizes between 8 and 24 pixels,
because a label is read by the size of its letters. A mapped `opacity` works the same way. The
smallest value is drawn at opacity 0.15, faint but visible, and the largest at
0.95:

```{r}
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + opacity(bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Fewer bronze medals, fainter name") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, opacity by
bronze."*

gog sets each channel's scale from every row of the layer, so one value draws at
the same size and opacity in every panel.

A word cloud also sizes each word by a value, but its positions carry no data:
each word is placed wherever there is room. In gog a label is drawn at its row's
`x` and `y`, and `repel` only moves it off its neighbors, so gog draws no word
cloud.

## Labels in the cube {#labels-in-the-cube}

A 3-D scatter has the same problem as a flat one: a dot does not say which row
it is. A label can be drawn in the [cube](../space.qmd), as a point can. Bind
`z`, and each label is drawn at the place its row's three positions give it.
Nearer labels are drawn over farther ones:

```{r}
data(medals) + point + text * repel + x(gold) + y(silver) + z(bronze) +
  label(country) + title("Each country at its three medal counts") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: points and also text derived by repel, x is gold, y is
silver, z is bronze, label by country."*

`repel` moves labels off each other and off the dots, as on a flat plot. A
nudge moves a label on the picture, not in the cube: `"up"` is toward the top of
the image at every angle.

## A halo around each label {#a-halo-around-each-label}

A label drawn over a dot or a line can be hard to read, because the mark shows
around its letters. `style(border_size = )` draws a **halo**: a band of the
panel's background color around each letter, drawn under the text. It hides the
mark next to each letter and does not change the letters:

```{r}
data(medals) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e", size = 9) +
  text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  style(size = 12, border_size = 3) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Names with a halo") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by
country, with size 12 and border size 3."*

A thin band of the panel's color now separates each name from the gray dot
behind it. `border_size` sets the width, in pixels, of the line drawn around each
letter to make the halo. Half of that line lies under the letters, so a width of
3 shows as a band 1.5 pixels wide.
`border_color` sets its color, if you want one other than the background. Either
setting alone draws a halo: an unset width is 3 pixels, and an unset color is the
panel's background color. With neither, a label has no halo.

A halo hides the marks it covers, so use it where the words matter more than
those marks. Within one layer it never hides another label's letters, because
every halo in a layer is drawn before any of that layer's letters. A `text`
layer written later is drawn on top, so its halos can cover the letters of an
earlier `text` layer. A halo does not move overlapping labels apart.
That is the job of [`repel`](#repel-moving-labels-off-each-other).

## Turning a label {#turning-a-label}

A note beside a vertical line is easiest to read when it is written along the
line, not across it. `style(angle = )` turns every label in its layer by the
number of degrees you give, counterclockwise from horizontal, so `90` reads
upward and `-90` downward. Each label turns around its own position, the point
its `x` and `y` give. The `milestones` table holds two notes. Each is drawn at
the income in `at` and the height in `value`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(milestones)
```

In this plot a vertical `rule` marks each income, and each note is drawn along
its rule:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  data(milestones) + rule + x(at) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  data(milestones) + text + x(at) + y(value) + label(note) +
  style(angle = 90, border_size = 3) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Notes turned 90 degrees") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life; then given
the milestones: rules, x is at; then given the milestones: text, x is at, y is
value, label by note, with angle 90."*

Each note is now parallel to its line, and the halo from the section above
hides the line behind its letters. gog measures a turned label by the space it
takes after turning, and `repel` uses that space to keep labels apart.

Three kinds of plot place each name inside a region: a sunburst, a nest and a
flow. A set angle works differently in each. With no angle set, a
[sunburst](../polar.qmd#naming-the-nodes) keeps most names upright. It turns a
name that is too wide for its sector, and shrinks it if it still does not fit. A
set angle turns every name by that angle instead, and draws it at full size. In
a [`nest`](../nest.qmd#naming-the-regions), a turned
name is drawn smaller until it fits its rectangle, as an upright name is. A
[flow](../flow.qmd#room-for-long-names) draws every name at full size, so
turning is how a long name stays inside its tall, narrow slot.

## Why `label` is a channel {#why-label-is-a-channel}

A setting is a value you type into the sentence. You might expect to type a
label into the sentence in the same way, like a title. A label is not a title:
it is one value per row, and that makes it data. One rule of the grammar decides
whether a label is a setting or a channel: data reaches a mark only through a
channel. That makes `label` a channel, so no mark takes the words themselves as
an argument. A fixed note is therefore a table with one row, given to `data()`,
and never a value given to `style()`.

Only `text` accepts `label`; every other mark refuses it, which is why a labeled
scatter is `point + text` and never a `label` on `point`. `text` *requires* a
`label`: the label is part of the mark's
[minimum syllable](../design-laws.qmd#law-7-minimum-syllable), as `x` and `y` are.
Ask for a text mark with no `label` and the engine refuses, and says what to
write instead, as [What it refuses](#what-it-refuses) shows. `text` is the mark,
and `label` is the channel that carries the column it draws.

## A note is a layer {#a-note-is-a-layer}

A plot often needs one note written on it, at a place you choose. It may say
what a region of the scatter means, or why a point is where it is. If you
have used ggplot2, a note there is a separate function, `annotate()`. In gog it
is a table with one row, and the plot below draws it. A second `data()` gives
the mark written right after it its own table ([Data](../data.qmd)), and a table
with one row in it puts one string on the plot:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(income_note)
```

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(income_note) + text + label(what) +
  title("A note is a layer, not a function") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also text from the
income note, label by what."*

The note is in an empty corner of the scatter: no country in 2007 has an
income that high with lives that short.

That plot needed nothing new in the grammar. A mark written directly after a
`data()` already reads that table, and `text` already draws one string per row.
The note is data like any other, so it is scaled like any other. Give the note
an `x` far from the points, and the axes stretch to cover it, so check the axes
each time you place a note.

One rule applies while writing a note. The `text` layer names no position of its
own, so it reads the columns the axes use, `gdp` and `life`, from its own table.
That is why `income_note` has a column with each of those names. When a note
table's columns have other names, write its positions after `text`, as [Turning
a label](#turning-a-label) does for the `milestones` table:
`+ text + x(at) + y(value) + label(note)`. Any other mark at a place you choose
is written the same way: a small table, and a layer over it. A dot on the plot
is a `point` over the same one-row table, and several notes are several rows.

## Text that a transform places {#text-that-a-transform-places}

You choose where a note goes. A transform can choose the place instead, and then
the text names whatever that transform built. In the first six rows, a second
layer with the same transform draws the shape the text labels:

| Text derived by | What it labels |
|---|---|
| `text * layout` | the nodes of a network, beside `point * layout` and `edge * layout` |
| `text * flow` | each stage's slots in a flow, beside `ribbon * flow` and `zone * flow` |
| `text * partition` | the regions of a hierarchy, beside `zone * partition` |
| `text * count`, `text * bin` | the count of each bar, beside `bar * count` or `bar * bin` ([Number labels](#number-labels-the-value-on-each-mark)) |
| `text * mean`, `text * sum` and the other summaries | the summary of each bar, beside `bar * mean` or `bar * sum` ([Number labels](#number-labels-the-value-on-each-mark)) |
| `text * dodge` | each group's bar in a slot, beside `bar * dodge` ([Labels on dodged bars](#labels-on-dodged-bars)) |
| `text * repel` | the scatter labels of [`repel`](#repel-moving-labels-off-each-other), moved off each other |

The chapters that draw the first three are [Network](../network.qmd), [Flow](../flow.qmd)
and [Transforms](../transforms.qmd#partition-a-whole-among-nested-parts). In each one the text is a layer over the mark that
drew the shape, and both layers read the same transform.

## Transforms it takes {#transforms-it-takes}

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values
instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a text mark takes
and the ones it refuses:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_transforms("text")
```

The plots below show every transform a text mark takes. Within a
figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each
figure names any other change. Every text layer needs `label()`. After a
transform, the label can print only a column that the new rows hold, as [Number
labels](#number-labels-the-value-on-each-mark) explains.

**Counting.** `count` and `proportion` tally the rows at each value of `x`, on a
category or a number. `bin` counts the rows in each interval of a number, and
`density` estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely the rows lie along it. Each
one writes its result into a column, `count`, `proportion` or `density`, and
`label()` prints that column. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty,
so a larger count is printed higher. The left and middle plots put `continent`
on `x`, and the right plot puts `life`. `decimals = 2` prints each proportion to
two decimal places:

```{r}
(data(gapminder_2007) + text * count + x(continent) + label(count) +
   title("text * count") +
   theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + text * proportion + x(continent) +
     label(proportion, decimals = 2) + title("text * proportion") +
     theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + text * bin + x(life) + label(count) +
     title("text * bin") +
     theme(background = "white"))
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: text derived by count, x is continent, label by count,
beside text derived by proportion, x is continent, label by proportion with 2
decimal places, beside text derived by bin, x is life, label by count."*

`density` gets a plot of its own, because its numbers need the full width of the
page. The curve is computed at 256 places unless you set `places`, and 256
numbers would print on top of each other. `density(places = 12)` computes it at 12, and each
number is the curve's height at one of them:

```{r}
data(gapminder_2007) + text * density(places = 12) + x(life) +
  label(density, decimals = 3) + title("text * density(places = 12)") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: text derived by density at 12 places, x is life, label
by density with 3 decimal places."*

A curve is easier to read as a stroke, `line * density`, as the
[`density`](../transforms.qmd#density-kernel-density-estimate) section of
Transforms shows.

**Summaries.** The six summaries reduce the rows at each value of `x` to one
value, so they need a number on `y`. `sum` reads `population`, because only an
amount has a total that means something. The other five read `life`. They give
the mean, the median, the largest and the smallest value, and `quantile(0.9)`
gives the value that nine tenths of the rows fall below. A summary writes its
value into the column it reads, so `label()` names that column:
`label(population, short = TRUE)` after `sum`, and `label(life, decimals = 1)`
after the other five. Each label is drawn above a bar with the same summary,
moved up by `style(nudge = "up")`. That is the usual way to label a summary:

```{r}
(((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +
     text * sum + label(population, short = TRUE) + style(nudge = "up") +
     title("text * sum") +
     theme(background = "white")) |
    (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
       text * mean + label(life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
       title("text * mean") +
       theme(background = "white"))) /
   ((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * median + x(continent) + y(life) +
       text * median + label(life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
       title("text * median") +
       theme(background = "white")) |
      (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * max + x(continent) + y(life) +
         text * max + label(life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
         title("text * max") +
         theme(background = "white"))) /
   ((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * min + x(continent) + y(life) +
       text * min + label(life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
       title("text * min") +
       theme(background = "white")) |
      (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * quantile(0.9) + x(continent) + y(life) +
         text * quantile(0.9) + label(life, decimals = 1) +
         style(nudge = "up") + title("text * quantile(0.9)") +
         theme(background = "white")))) +
  theme(height = 1100)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum, x is continent, y is population,
and also text derived by sum, label by population written short, beside bars
derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, and also text derived by mean, label
by life with 1 decimal place; above bars derived by median, x is continent, y is
life, and also text derived by median, label by life with 1 decimal place,
beside bars derived by max, x is continent, y is life, and also text derived by
max, label by life with 1 decimal place; above bars derived by min, x is
continent, y is life, and also text derived by min, label by life with 1 decimal
place, beside bars derived by quantile at 0.9, x is continent, y is life, and
also text derived by quantile at 0.9, label by life with 1 decimal place."*

The five plots that read `life` share one scale, so their bars can be compared
from plot to plot, and each label prints the value, to one decimal place.

**Running total.** `cumulative` adds each value to the ones before it along the
axis. It writes the total to a column named `cumulative`, and
`label(cumulative)` prints it. The `actuals` table holds one year of sales in
each row:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(actuals)
```

```{r}
data(actuals) + text * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) + label(cumulative) +
  title("text * cumulative") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the actuals: text derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales, label by
cumulative."*

The last label, 703, is the total of all five years. The rows still hold each
year's own `sales`, so `label(sales)` would print 168 at the same place.

**Collision modifiers.** Collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on
top of one another. `dodge` sets the groups in one slot side by side, so it
needs a split, such as `color` or `group`. The top plot prints each
continent's mean life expectancy in 1957 and in 2007, from the `gm_eras` table
shown in [Labels on dodged bars](#labels-on-dodged-bars). `repel` moves each
label off the other labels. The bottom plot names the ten countries of
`gm_populous`, shown in [`repel`: moving labels off each
other](#repel-moving-labels-off-each-other), with `gdp` on `x` and `life` on
`y`:

```{r}
((data(gm_eras) + text * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
    label(life, decimals = 1) + title("text * mean * dodge") +
    theme(background = "white")) /
   (data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
      title("text * repel") +
      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(height = 900)
```

*"Given the gapminder eras: text derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is
life, color by era, label by life with 1 decimal place; above text from the ten
most populous countries, derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by
country."*

**Layouts.** `partition`, `flow` and `layout` each build a whole picture from
the rows, and each writes the name of every part into a column called `name`. A
text layer with the same transform prints each name with `label(name)`, at the
place where another layer draws that part. `partition` splits a whole into
nested parts, such as a budget into groups and items, so it needs a hierarchy of
categorical columns. `flow` splits an amount at each of a series of stages,
such as each person's class on the Titanic and then whether they survived, so it needs one column for each
stage. `layout` is for tables that record relations rather than measurements:
each row says that one name is related to another, and no column gives a name a
position. So `layout` computes a position for each name, and it needs two
columns of names and the network space, `network()`. The partition sizes each
part by `amount` on `x`, and the flow by `n` on `y`. The three tables are these.
`spending` holds a household budget. `titanic` counts the people on the Titanic
by class, sex, age and whether they survived, with one row for each combination
and the count in `n`. `trade_partners` has one row for each trade relation,
naming who exports and who imports:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(spending)
peek(titanic)
peek(trade_partners)
```

```{r}
((data(spending) + x(amount) + zone * partition(group, item) + color(group) +
    text * partition(group, item) + label(name) + style(angle = 90) +
    title("text * partition, with the zones") +
    theme(background = "white")) /
   (data(titanic) + y(n) + ribbon * flow(class, survived) +
      zone * flow(class, survived) + text * flow(class, survived) +
      label(name) + title("text * flow, with the bands and the slots") +
      theme(background = "white")) /
   (data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
      text * layout(exporter, importer) + label(name) +
      style(border_size = 3) + network() +
      title("text * layout, with the edges") +
      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(height = 1500)
```

*"Given the spending table: x is amount, zones derived by partition through
group and item, colored by group, and also text derived by partition through
group and item, label by name; above ribbons from titanic, derived by flow
through class and survived, y is n, and also zones derived by flow through class
and survived, and text derived by flow through class and survived, label by
name; above edges from trade partners, derived by layout from exporter to
importer, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer, label by
name, in the network."*

The names on the partition are turned with `style(angle = 90)`, as in [Turning a
label](#turning-a-label), so that each fits its narrow region. The names in the
network have a [halo](#a-halo-around-each-label), which hides the edges behind
their letters.

A text mark refuses every transform in the Refuses column above. `smooth` and
`straight` compute a line at evenly spaced places along `x`, not at the values
in your rows. A label there would print no value from your table.
A [`line`](line.qmd) draws the fitted values instead. The pair transforms give `y` a low and a high at
each value of `x`, two numbers where a label prints one.
[`interval`](interval.qmd) and [`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd) draw the pair, and
`text * max` or `text * min` prints one end of a `range`. `stack` piles up bars,
areas and the dots of a dot plot, and `jitter` moves each point a short way
along the categorical axis. Neither measures the space a label's letters take.
`repel` does, so it is the collision modifier for labels. `cluster` joins the
closest categories into a tree, which [`path`](path.qmd) draws.

## What you can set {#what-you-can-set}

The [Styling](#styling-one-color-one-size) section set a color and a size. Those
are two entries in a longer list, and the whole of it is here: which color, how
transparent, which size, which way to shift the label, by how many degrees to turn it, and
the color and width of its halo. A setting gives one value to every label in
the layer. Three of them, `color`, `size` and `opacity`, can instead be mapped
from a column, as the sections above show. Each mark takes its own settings.
[Setting vs mapping](../style.qmd) shows how a setting differs from mapping a
column. These are a text mark's settings, with the values each accepts:

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
mark_options("text")
```

`nudge` and `angle` are the two settings only `text` has. `nudge` exists so a
layered `point + text` does not draw the label on top of the dot. The plot uses
the `medals` table, shown in [The mark and its
content](#the-mark-and-its-content):

```{r}
data(medals) + x(country) + y(gold) +
  point + style(color = "#9e9e9e", size = 6) +
  text + label(gold) + style(nudge = "up", size = 11, color = "black") +
  y_label("Gold medals") + title("Labels nudged off their points") +
  theme(background = "white")
```

*"Given the medals: x is country, y is gold, points colored #9e9e9e, with size
6, and also text, label by gold, colored black, with nudge up and size 11."*

Each count is just above its dot, and neither covers the other. The four
directions, and how far a nudge moves a label, are under [Nudging the label off
its point](#nudging-the-label-off-its-point), with `repel` for labels that
collide with each other.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

A text mark always refuses four things: a missing `label`, the `shape` channel,
any `pattern`, and a continuous column on `color`. It refuses `group` only when
no statistic and no `dodge` uses it. The label is part of the mark's minimum
syllable, as `x` and `y` are: with no string, a text mark has nothing to draw.
The engine refuses and names the channel to add:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver)
```

A reader who knows `point` will try its channels on `text`. `size` and `opacity`
draw with a continuous column, as on a point. `color` draws only with a
categorical column, unlike a point, which takes either kind. A continuous column
on `color` is refused, and the message names `size` or `opacity` to show it
instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + color(bronze)
```

`shape` is refused outright, because it cannot change a string. A point's glyph
can change shape because the dot itself says nothing. A text mark's glyph is the
string itself, so there is nothing for `shape` to change:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + shape(country)
```

A string takes no texture either. `pattern` sets the texture of a stroke or of a
filled region, and a word is neither:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  style(pattern = "hatch")
```

On a `text` layer, `group` splits the rows that a statistic summarizes or that
`dodge` sets side by side ([Labels on dodged bars](#labels-on-dodged-bars)). A
`text` layer with neither draws one label for each row, so `group` has nothing to
split. A scatter has no categorical axis, so it has no bars for the labels to be
printed above, and gog suggests `color` instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + group(country)
```

## In short {#in-short}

A text mark will not draw without a `label`, and no other mark accepts one. Its
words come from a column, so a fixed note is a table with one row. `repel`
draws every label and reports how many still overlap, because which names to
leave out is your decision.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

Without `repel`, row order never moves a word: each one is drawn at the position
its own row gives it. For a [path](path.qmd), row order decides which rows are
joined: the mark joins each row to the next, in the order the table holds them.
